summary: A 1911 concrete light on a remote Lake Superior island, its 1886 wooden predecessor, keepers from 1887, and the loss of the Lambton (1922 or 1923); best seen by boat or from the air.

light.remarks: Marked seasonal on the Canadian Coast Guard list (Lake Superior, entry 1096).

lens.where: Canadian Coast Guard base, Parry Sound

structures.type: hexagonal reinforced concrete, six flying buttresses
structures.note: First shown 1912. Coast Guard list gives structure height 35.1 m; Lighthouse Friends gives 104 ft (about 32 m) base to vane.
Replaced by the concrete tower; 80 ft base to vane in the Department's 1886 description.
100 ft south of the first tower; compressed-air horn.

staffing.note: Reg Dawson keeper in 1968. The date resident keepers ended is not in these sources; the Register describes the lantern as fully automated (1991).

access.note: Canadian Coast Guard property. Grounds open, tower closed. Best seen by boat or from the air.

events.note: Parliament funds a lighthouse and fog trumpet; $6,475 contract to John George and David Currie of Port Elgin.
Wooden octagonal tower; in operation 26 August 1886.
Compressed-air horn, five-second blast every 30 seconds.
Midland Queen and Ottawa collided off the island in dense fog. Date disputed: 14 October per the Department; a newspaper reported it 8 October.
Tugs Reid and Boynton brought keeper Demers and helper Fred Pelletier back from the island in December.
Five-inch duplicate diaphone installed in the fog-alarm building.
Reinforced concrete tower, 80 ft (24 m), in the Department's works list for the year.
Second-order dioptric light, group of three flashes every ten seconds, replaced the revolving white light (Lighthouse Friends). Later Coast Guard list: single flash every ten seconds.

C.G.S. Lambton lost with all hands off Caribou island in a severe storm, 19 April. Date disputed: the Department's report for the fiscal year 1922-23 (July 1922 to June 1923) implies April 1923; Lighthouse Friends says 18-19 April 1922.
Radiobeacon established, synchronized with the foghorn; flashing electric winter light placed on the gallery.
Five radar reflectors mounted near the gallery; served until 1955.
Classified Federal Heritage Building; recognized by the Government of Canada 30 September 1991.
Light station solarized with a 12-volt DC rotating beacon; lens removed from service and now on display at the Coast Guard base in Parry Sound.

corrections.why: The Canadian Register (entry 10361) gives the date recognized as 30 September 1991. The record's 1990 comes from Wikidata.
The record's tower of 1886 was the first, wooden octagonal tower (Lighthouse Friends). The concrete tower now standing is dated 1911 by the Register, and was first shown in 1912.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Both 1886 and 1912 are right for different towers. The wooden octagonal tower was first lit on 26 August 1886 (Lighthouse Friends, from the Department's description). The concrete tower was built in 1911 and its light first shown on the opening of navigation in 1912 (Register; Lighthouse Friends).

notes_for_editor: Sources read: Register text (via Heritage Guide), Lighthouse Friends (copyrighted; facts paraphrased, one short quotation at most per sentence), the Canadian Coast Guard list, Department of Marine reports in the corpus (fiscal 1900, 1905, 1910, 1911, 1923), Minneapolis Journal 27 Dec 1904, Superior Times 8 Oct 1904, and the 1923 Lighthouse Service Bulletin. Wikipedia and Wikidata were read as leads only and are not cited. OCR matched by position: the 1899 appointment of Wilbrod Demers (fiscal 1900 statement, p. 122), which also appears in the fiscal 1903 table; the Department's 1914-15 keepers' table (identifier 1915v50, scan p. 74) has a Caribou entry for 'J. W. Johnston' (OCR 'Johnflton'), not used: it may or may not be George W. Johnston. Keepers 1886-1921 and 1922-1968 come from Lighthouse Friends alone, since the corpus holds Canadian reports only from fiscal 1900 and the later keeper lists were not read in primary sources; check against the 1912-1921 Department statements if they are digitised. The assistant lost with Penfold is unnamed in the sources and left off the roster. The Department paragraph on the Lambton gives April 18 and 19 without a year; the year 1922 is from Lighthouse Friends. Disagreements left open: the Midland Queen-Ottawa collision date (14 October per the Department; a newspaper reported it on 8 October); the 1912 characteristic (three flashes per ten seconds per Lighthouse Friends; one flash per ten seconds per the Coast Guard list, which also marks the light seasonal); tower height (104 ft base to vane per Lighthouse Friends; 35.1 m structure height per the Coast Guard list; 31.5 m in the station record). Heritage date: the record says 1990, the Register says recognized 30 September 1991. Staffing end date is not in these sources. The Lighthouse Service Bulletin passage gives August 7 with no year; the volume is 1923. Lighthouse Friends gives the distance from the mainland as forty miles; the story gives forty miles (about 64 km), not the nautical-mile figure this record had. Photos: none added (record photo is a Wikimedia Commons file, not checked). Fact-check 2026-10-27: the Lambton report (Department of Marine and Fisheries, fiscal year 1922-23, scan p. 112) puts the loss in April 1923 by its own fiscal year; Lighthouse Friends gives 18-19 April 1922. The story states both and does not settle it. The roster dates for Penfold (1921-1922) and Kennedy (1922-1928) follow Lighthouse Friends and would move if the loss was in 1923. 'Thunder Bay District' was removed from the opening: no cited source gives it, and the Coast Guard's Thunder Bay entries are at about 48 N, well north-west of Caribou Island (about 47.3 N, 85.8 W). The 1900 Demers row (scan 219) and the 1911 Caribou works row (scan 69) were confirmed on the page images, so the position matches are now image-checked.
